subject: Geography
title: Water Sources and Management
learningOutcomes: Identify the major sources of water on Earth and in Pakistan (salty water and freshwater).
Explain the different types of precipitation — rain, snow, hail and sleet.
Describe the process of the water cycle in maintaining the Earth's water supply.
Identify the different uses of reclaimed sewage waste water and ways to increase the water supply.
Identify biogas as a renewable source of energy and explain how it is produced.
Describe how water is conserved through education and technology.

sections.heading: Water Supply
sections.body: Water is an important natural resource found on Earth in two forms — salty (sea) water and freshwater. About 70% of the Earth's surface is covered by water, which is why Earth is called the Blue Planet. The seas and oceans hold about 97% of this water as salt water, which is not fit for drinking or agriculture. Only about 3% is freshwater, and most of it is locked away: about 79% is in ice caps and glaciers, about 20% is groundwater, and only about 1% is easily-available surface water in rivers, streams and lakes. The three main sources of freshwater are ice and snow in glaciers, rivers and lakes on the surface, and ground water below the surface.

sections.heading: Precipitation and Its Types
sections.body: Precipitation is the falling of water from the sky. It occurs as rain (liquid droplets 0.5 mm or larger; smaller droplets are drizzle), snow (flakes of ice), hail (big, irregular, purely solid lumps of ice) and sleet (small, semitransparent balls of ice, smaller than hail). Precipitation is unevenly distributed because of constant heating and the global circulation of air — tropical regions receive high rainfall while desert regions receive very little, so many water-scarce countries lie in Africa and the Middle East.

sections.heading: The Water Cycle
sections.body: The water cycle (hydrological cycle) is the continuous movement of water from the atmosphere to the land and back again. It has four processes: precipitation, evaporation, transpiration and condensation. Rain falls and flows as surface runoff or infiltrates into the groundwater. The Sun's heat evaporates water into vapour, plants add vapour through transpiration, and the rising vapour cools and condenses into clouds, which fall again as precipitation. Energy from the Sun drives the whole cycle.

sections.heading: Rising Demand and Ways to Increase Supply
sections.body: The demand for water is rising due to population growth, agriculture (which uses about 69% of freshwater) and industrialisation (cooling machinery and hydroelectric power). Households use about 7% of freshwater. Supply can be increased by reclaiming used (sewage) water — purifying it to remove solids, bacteria and impurities so it can be reused — by careful catchment-area management, and by desalination, which removes salt from seawater through distillation or membrane filtration.

sections.heading: Biogas and Water Conservation
sections.body: Biogas is a renewable, environmentally friendly gas made when organic waste (food scraps and animal waste) is decomposed by bacteria through anaerobic respiration in an airtight biodigester; it is used as vehicle fuel and for cooking and heating. Water conservation means reducing the use and wastage of water. It is achieved through education (teaching people the value of water) and technology (water-saving gadgets on taps and toilets, and improved irrigation).

definitions.definition: Water without a significant amount of salt; drinkable and used for domestic purposes, agriculture and industries.
The falling of water from the sky in the form of rain, snow, hail or sleet.
The continuous movement of water from the atmosphere to the land and back to the atmosphere.
The change of a liquid into water vapour.
The process in which plants give off moisture into the atmosphere.
The change of water vapour into water, forming clouds.
The layer of water found under the layers of rocks below the surface of the Earth.
Purifying used (sewage) water so that it can be used again.
The removal of salt from seawater to obtain freshwater.
A gas produced when organic waste is broken down by bacteria through anaerobic respiration.
Reducing the use and wastage of water to save water resources.

examTips: Remember the key figures: about 97% of Earth's water is salt water and only 3% is freshwater; of the freshwater, 79% is in glaciers, 20% is groundwater and only 1% is surface water.
The four processes of the water cycle are precipitation, evaporation, transpiration and condensation — and the Sun drives the cycle.
Don't confuse the ways to INCREASE supply (reclamation, desalination, catchment management, conservation) with the REASONS for rising demand (population, agriculture, industrialisation).
Hail is purely solid and larger; sleet is small, semitransparent ice; rain is liquid (0.5 mm or larger) and drizzle is smaller than 0.5 mm.
